origins: A serious diagnosis or permanent change can feel like the end of the life we knew: work, plans, roles, and dreams. Grief for that life is real. But grief can slide into believing that nothing meaningful remains.
teaches: “For I know the plans I have for you,” declares the LORD (Jeremiah 29:11). Paul writes, “Therefore we do not lose heart… our light and momentary affliction is producing for us an eternal weight of glory.” “In old age they will still bear fruit” (Psalm 92:14), and the psalmist asks God not to forsake him “until I proclaim Your power to the next generation.” Your old life may be over, but your life is not. God is not finished with you.
self_statements: There is nothing left to live for.
I am just waiting for the end.
errors: Believing life is either full or over.
Feeling devastated and concluding that life is finished.
questions: What exactly have I lost, and what remains?
What new things could I still do or give, even in small ways?
Who needs what I can still offer?
What does Scripture say about God’s plans and purposes?
What would I tell a friend in my situation?
What is one meaningful thing I can do this week?
truth: A season of my life may have ended, but my life has not. God is not finished with me, and He can give new purpose and meaning in my new circumstances. If hopeless thoughts become heavy, I will reach out for help right away.
hw_truths: God will finish the work He began.
log: Each week, note one meaningful thing you did or gave.
actions: Write what you can still do.
If you think of ending your life, call or text 988 (U.S.) now.
prayer: Father, a life I knew has ended. Comfort my grief, and show me the purposes You still have for me. Do not let me lose heart. Amen.
